input.title: OpenAI provider emits Finish before Usage, violating the core event-ordering contract
input.description:
Found while designing SMA-451 (LiteLLM provider) and verified against a live OpenAI-compatible proxy.

## The defect

`paigasus_helikon_core::Model::invoke`'s contract states plainly (`crates/paigasus-helikon-core/src/model.rs:63`):

> `Finish` is the terminal event; nothing follows it.

`ChatTranslator::consume` in `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-openai/src/backend/chat.rs:238-241` buffers the finish reason and emits `Finish` **inline, at the end of the chunk that carried `finish_reason`**.

But with `stream_options.include_usage: true`, the usage snapshot does **not** arrive on that chunk. It arrives in a **separate trailing chunk after it**. Captured verbatim from LiteLLM 1.97.0 serving the OpenAI Chat Completions wire shape:

```
data: {…"choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{},"finish_reason":"stop"}]}
data: {…"choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{}}],"usage":{"completion_tokens":6,"prompt_tokens":8,"total_tokens":14,"completion_tokens_details":{"reasoning_tokens":0}}}
data: [DONE]
```

So the provider emits `Finish` and then `Usage` — on **every streaming turn**, not as an edge case.

## Why it matters

Any consumer that stops reading at `Finish` (which the contract explicitly licenses) drops the only usage snapshot of the turn. The agent loop's cross-turn token summing (SMA-402) then silently under-counts every OpenAI turn.

## Why the tests don't catch it

The fixtures encode a wire shape that does not occur. `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-openai/tests/fixtures/chat_parallel_tool_calls.txt` puts `usage` on the **same** chunk as `finish_reason`:

```
data: {"id":"x",…,"choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{},"finish_reason":"tool_calls"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":10,…}}
```

Against that fixture the inline-`Finish` implementation looks correct. A test written against it would pass on broken code.

The Responses backend (`backend/responses.rs`) should be checked for the same pattern.

## Suggested fix

Adopt the pattern already shipping in the Gemini provider: buffer the finish reason and emit `Finish` from a dedicated `finish()` call at `[DONE]`/EOF.

- `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini/src/stream.rs:73-87` — `finish()`, which emits nothing when no finish reason was observed (so a truncated stream is not reported as a clean `Stop`).
- `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini/src/model.rs:150,156` — the two call sites (`[DONE]` and EOF).

Then **re-record the fixtures from real traffic** so `usage` sits on its own trailing chunk, and add a regression test asserting `Finish` is the last event and `Usage` precedes it. Re-recording is the important half: fixing the translator while leaving hand-written fixtures in place would leave the same blind spot for the next change.

## Reproduction

No OpenAI key needed — a keyless LiteLLM proxy reproduces the wire shape:

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: mock-fast
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/gpt-4o-mini
      api_key: fake-key
      mock_response: "Hello from the mock backend."
general_settings: {master_key: REDACTED}
```

```bash
docker run -d --name litellm-probe -p 4000:4000 \
  -v "$PWD/litellm-config.yaml:/app/config.yaml" \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable --config /app/config.yaml --port 4000

curl -sN http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Authorization: Bearer REDACTED' \
  -d '{"model":"mock-fast","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],
       "stream":true,"stream_options":{"include_usage":true}}'
```

Full evidence: Appendix B of `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-16-sma-451-litellm-provider-design.md` (on the SMA-451 branch).

input.title: Add a signal-only litellm-it CI job using a keyless LiteLLM container
input.description:
Follow-up from SMA-451. Blocked by SMA-451 landing (the crate and its `tests/live.rs` must exist first).

## Why

SMA-451's design initially asserted that a live LiteLLM CI job "needs a container plus at least one real upstream key", so it could never be more than a loud-skip. **That premise is false and was retracted.**

LiteLLM's `mock_response` deployments serve full streaming SSE, real router fallbacks, and real LiteLLM error envelopes with `api_key: fake-key`. The entire verification rig behind SMA-451's Appendix B ran **without any upstream credential**.

This matters because that rig caught two defects that both a careful design pass and an adversarial spec review had missed:

1. `usage` arrives in a **separate trailing chunk after** the `finish_reason` chunk — the design would have violated core's `Finish`-is-terminal contract on every turn. (Also a live bug in the OpenAI provider — SMA-522.)
2. `error.code` is the **HTTP status as a string** (`"400"`, `"429"`, `"500"`), not a semantic code — so the designed primary classification signal could never have matched anything.

Both are wire-shape facts that only real traffic reveals. Wiremock tests assert what we *think* the wire looks like; this job would assert what it *is*.

## Scope

Add a `litellm-it` job to `.github/workflows/integration.yml`, following the `temporal-it` pattern already established there:

- **Signal-only**: not listed in `.github/rulesets/main-protection-checks.json`. Signal-only means *not required*, never `continue-on-error` — that would report green unconditionally and destroy the signal.
- **Step-level `if:` guards, not job-level.** A skipped job reports no status at all, which blocks every PR the moment the context is promoted. Same reasoning as `sessions-it`.
- Boot `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable` (pin the digest; nothing tracks this automatically — it joins `TEMPORAL_CLI_VERSION` and `NIGHTLY_TOOLCHAIN` as a hand-bumped pin) with a `mock_response` config, and probe readiness on `/health/liveliness`.
- Run `tests/live.rs` with an env var that turns its loud-skip into a **panic**, mirroring `HELIKON_REQUIRE_TEMPORAL` / `HELIKON_REQUIRE_SANDBOX`. Without it a job that never reached the proxy is indistinguishable from a green one, because a skipped test passes and `cargo test` captures its output.
- Reuse the config in Appendix B of `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-16-sma-451-litellm-provider-design.md`.

## What this can and cannot cover

**Can**: streaming chunk ordering and shape, usage field presence, error envelope structure and status codes, `fallbacks`/`num_retries`/`metadata.tags` acceptance and routing, URL/auth handling, `x-litellm-*` response headers.

**Cannot**: anything requiring a real backend — streaming tool-call `index` presence, reasoning-field naming (`reasoning_content` vs `reasoning` vs `thinking_blocks`), and true mid-stream error frames. These are listed as open unknowns in SMA-451 §17 and stay open.

## Promotion

Same bar as `temporal-it`: ≥ 20 executed runs with ≤ 1 flake, or 30 consecutive green nightlies, before adding it to `main-protection-checks.json` and CONTRIBUTING.md's required-contexts table.

2. `error.code` is the **HTTP status as a string** (`"400"`, `"429"`, `"500"`), not a semantic code — so the designed primary classification signal could never have matched anything.

Both are wire-shape facts that only real traffic reveals. Wiremock tests assert what we *think* the wire looks like; this job would assert what it *is*.

## Scope

Add a `litellm-it` job to `.github/workflows/integration.yml`, following the `temporal-it` pattern already established there:

* **Signal-only**: not listed in `.github/rulesets/main-protection-checks.json`. Signal-only means *not required*, never `continue-on-error` — that would report green unconditionally and destroy the signal.
* **Step-level** `if:` **guards, not job-level.** A skipped job reports no status at all, which blocks every PR the moment the context is promoted. Same reasoning as `sessions-it`.
* Boot `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable` (pin the digest; nothing tracks this automatically — it joins `TEMPORAL_CLI_VERSION` and `NIGHTLY_TOOLCHAIN` as a hand-bumped pin) with a `mock_response` config, and probe readiness on `/health/liveliness`.
* Run `tests/live.rs` with an env var that turns its loud-skip into a **panic**, mirroring `HELIKON_REQUIRE_TEMPORAL` / `HELIKON_REQUIRE_SANDBOX`. Without it a job that never reached the proxy is indistinguishable from a green one, because a skipped test passes and `cargo test` captures its output.
* Reuse the config in Appendix B of `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-16-sma-451-litellm-provider-design.md`.

## What this can and cannot cover

**Can**: streaming chunk ordering and shape, usage field presence, error envelope structure and status codes, `fallbacks`/`num_retries`/`metadata.tags` acceptance and routing, URL/auth handling, `x-litellm-*` response headers.

**Cannot**: anything requiring a real backend — streaming tool-call `index` presence, reasoning-field naming (`reasoning_content` vs `reasoning` vs `thinking_blocks`), and true mid-stream error frames. These are listed as open unknowns in <issue id="3ff83fb5-f03b-4518-920a-a7ba0ec8d3e8" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-451/provider-crate-paigasus-helikon-providers-litellm">SMA-451</issue> §17 and stay open.

## Promotion

Same bar as `temporal-it`: ≥ 20 executed runs with ≤ 1 flake, or 30 consecutive green nightlies, before adding it to `main-protection-checks.json` and CONTRIBUTING.md's required-contexts table.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-523/add-a-signal-only-litellm-it-ci-job-using-a-keyless-litellm-container","gitBranchName":"feature/sma-523-add-a-signal-only-litellm-it-ci-job-using-a-keyless-litellm","createdAt":"2026-08-16T08:19:19.182Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-16T08:19:19.182Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["area:providers"],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Sven Maschek","createdById":"ba6021cb-56c5-43aa-9797-fab3599d7ead","project":"Paigasus Helikon","projectId":"5d1fd72d-af2d-40f5-b562-fa04f8018610","team":"Sven Maschek","teamId":"7178572e-d61f-4cf0-bbcb-4e03c8d9f39e"}

---
name: feedback-verify-provider-wire-with-container
description: Spin up the real service in Docker to verify wire-format claims before finalising a provider spec — don't defer it as a "release gate"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

When speccing a provider/adapter against an external HTTP service, **stand the service up in Docker and measure the wire format** rather than reasoning from vendor docs. Sven corrected me on this in SMA-451 (2026-08-16): I had written "this pipeline has no LiteLLM deployment, so verification is deferred to a release gate", and he replied *"you can spin up litellm in docker to verify"*.

**Why:** the probes falsified four claims that had already survived a careful design pass **and** an adversarial Opus spec review:

1. With `stream_options.include_usage`, `usage` arrives in a **separate trailing chunk after** the `finish_reason` chunk — so an inline-`Finish` translator violates core's "Finish is terminal" contract on *every* turn. (Same latent bug found in the shipped OpenAI provider → [[SMA-522]].)
2. LiteLLM's `error.code` is the **HTTP status as a string** (`"400"`/`"429"`/`"500"`), not a semantic code; `error.type` is `null` or the literal string `"None"`. Any classifier keying on `code == "context_length_exceeded"` matches nothing.
3. A failing *streaming* request returns `HTTP 500` + `content-type: application/json` — **not** an SSE error frame. Check status/content-type before entering the framing loop.
4. Unknown request params do **not** 400 at the proxy (even with `drop_params: false`), invalidating a "risks a 400" justification.

**How to apply:** most of these services mock without credentials — LiteLLM's `mock_response` deployments serve full streaming SSE, router fallbacks, and real error envelopes with `api_key: fake-key`. So "we'd need a real API key" is usually false; check before accepting it as a constraint. Capture the traces and **transcribe fixtures from them** — hand-written fixtures encode the shape you assumed (that is exactly how the OpenAI provider's bug survived). Record the evidence in a spec appendix with the image digest and version so claims are auditable. If the mock genuinely can't reach something (tool-call `index` presence, reasoning field names), say so explicitly rather than assuming.

Related: [[feedback-verify-merged-tree-not-relayed-output]], [[feedback-security-tests-assert-indistinguishability]].

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/smaschek/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

| 6 | Extras + request assembly | `build_request` + 9 insta snapshots + reserved-set exhaustiveness test |
| 7 | SSE types + `ChatTranslator` | Deferred `finish()`, tool-call state machine — 17 tests |
| 8 | Error classification | `classify()` keyed on the **measured** envelope |
| 9 | `Model` impl | HTTP + SSE loop, status/content-type check, correlation logging |
| 10 | Integration tests | Fixtures transcribed from captured traffic |
| 11 | Facade wiring + parity test | The cross-crate test that can actually detect drift |
| 12 | Documentation | 6 files, incl. the two stale "Four adapters" counts |
| 13 | CI gate reproduction | Full local run + `cargo publish --dry-run` |

**Three things I built in deliberately**, because they're where this work is most likely to go wrong:

- **Task 10 Step 8 is a mutation check.** It instructs the implementer to temporarily break the auth code and confirm the "no `Authorization` header" test *fails*. Wiremock has no negative header matcher, so that assertion is vacuous unless it's written against `received_requests()` — and vacuous is indistinguishable from passing.
- **Task 4 ports the OpenAI crate's tests along with its code.** Copying 345 lines without their tests is how duplication silently drifts; Task 11's cross-crate parity test is the other half.
- **Task 7's tests assert `Finish` is *not* emitted inline**, and Task 10's fixture puts `usage` in a trailing chunk. Those are the two assertions the original design would have failed.

I also flagged two spots where the plan itself is likely to fight the implementer (Task 2's URL segment manipulation, Task 11's helper), with the intended fallback for each.

---

**Execution mode:** I recommend **subagent-driven** — 13 tasks across a new crate, each with an independent test cycle, is exactly what it's for. Inline execution would put ~4k lines of generated code through one context with no review boundaries.

One thing I'll add to every dispatch: an explicit instruction to run `cargo test`/`build` **synchronously in the foreground** and not end the turn until the task reaches a terminal state. Implementer subagents in this repo have previously offloaded long cargo runs to a background monitor and then stopped mid-task, leaving a test written with no implementation.

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are: BLOCKED status you cannot resolve, ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" [shape=diamond];
        "Finding conflicts with plan text?" [shape=diamond];
        "Ask human partner which governs" [shape=box];
        "Fix round R of 5: R≤3 resume implementer; R≥4 fresh implementer, more capable model" [shape=box];
        "Dispatch scoped re-review (./re-review-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "All findings addressed?" [shape=diamond];
        "R = 5?" [shape=diamond];
        "Adjudicate each open finding" [shape=box];
        "Any load-bearing finding?" [shape=diamond];

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: STOP. Append `Task <N>: BLOCKED — <reason>` and report to
  your human partner with the finding, the plan text it collides with, and
  the fix history. Parking a structural failure lets every dependent task
  build on it and hands the final review a problem it cannot fix either.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or stop on load-bearing ones. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |

Checked `paigasus-helikon-core/src/model.rs:100-154`: `ModelRequest` = `messages`/`tools`/`model_settings`, and `ModelSettings` = `temperature`, `top_p`, `max_output_tokens` (→ `max_tokens`), `tool_choice`, `response_format`, `previous_response_id` (Responses-only, not emitted on Chat Completions). - The existing test cannot catch either: it uses a credential-free base URL and sets nothing in `extras`.
- *Fix*: in `Config::fmt`, render `endpoint` through a parse that blanks `username()`/`password()`, and print `extras.metadata` / `extras.extra_body` as key lists (or `<N entries>`) rather than values. **Important 2 — an empty-string env var is treated as *present* for fallback purposes, then dropped, so it blocks the next var in the chain.** `builder.rs:261-265` and `builder.rs:272-278`.

`std::env::var` returns `Ok("")` for a var set to empty, which `.ok()` turns into `Some("")`, satisfying `or_else` before your `.filter` ever runs. # Scoped Re-Review Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching a re-review after a fix round. The
re-reviewer verifies the findings were addressed and checks the fix diff for
new breakage. It is not a fresh review — the full review already happened.

**Purpose:** Verify each finding from the previous review was addressed, and
that the fix itself broke nothing.

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Re-review Task N fix round R"
  model: [MODEL — REQUIRED: choose per SKILL.md Model Selection; an omitted
         model silently inherits the session's most expensive one]
  prompt: |
    You are re-reviewing one task's fix round. A previous review produced
    findings; an implementer has attempted to fix them. Your job is to
    verdict each finding and inspect the fix diff — nothing else.

    ## The Task

    Read the task brief: [BRIEF_FILE]

    ## The Findings Under Verification

    [FINDINGS]

    ## The Fix

    Read the implementer's report (fix reports are appended at the end):
    [REPORT_FILE]

    **Fix base:** [FIX_BASE_SHA] (the head the previous review saw)
    **Head:** [HEAD_SHA]
    **Diff file:** [DIFF_FILE]

    Read the diff file once — it contains the fix commits, a stat summary,
    and the fix diff with surrounding context. Do not re-run git commands.
    If the diff file is missing, fetch the diff yourself:
    `git diff --stat [FIX_BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]` and
    `git diff [FIX_BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]`.

    Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working
    tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way.

    ## Scope

    Your scope is the findings list and the fix diff. Verdict every finding.
    Inspect the fix diff for new problems the fix itself introduced. Do NOT
    re-review code the fix did not touch: if you notice an issue entirely
    outside the fix diff, report it under Out-of-Scope Observations — it
    does not block this task and does not extend the loop. A broad
    whole-branch review happens after all tasks are complete.

    ## Tests

    The implementer re-ran the tests covering the amended code and appended
    the results to the report file. Treat the report as unverified claims:
    confirm the fix report names the covering tests and shows their output,
    and verify the claims against the diff. Do not re-run the suite to
    confirm their report. Run a test only when reading the code raises a
    specific doubt that no existing run answers — and then a focused test,
    never a package-wide suite.

    ## Output Format

    Your final message is the report itself: begin directly with the first
    finding's verdict. Every line is a verdict, a finding with file:line,
    or a check you ran — no preamble, no process narration.

    ### Finding Verdicts

    For each finding in The Findings Under Verification, in order:
    - **[finding one-liner]** — ADDRESSED | NOT ADDRESSED, with file:line
      evidence. "Attempted" is not addressed: the specific defect must no
      longer exist.

    ### New Breakage in the Fix Diff

    Anything the fix itself broke or introduced, with severity
    (Critical/Important/Minor) and file:line. "None" if clean.

    ### Out-of-Scope Observations

    Issues you noticed entirely outside the fix diff. Non-blocking; the
    controller ledgers these for the final review. "None" if none.

    ### Verdict

    **Fix round:** [All findings addressed, no new Critical/Important
    breakage | Findings remain open] — list the open ones.
```

**Placeholders:**
- `[MODEL]` — REQUIRED: reviewer model per SKILL.md Model Selection; scoped
  re-reviews of small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier
- `[BRIEF_FILE]` — the task brief file (same file the implementer worked from)
- `[FINDINGS]` — the Critical/Important findings and spec gaps from the
  previous review, copied verbatim, one per bullet
- `[REPORT_FILE]` — the implementer's report file (fix reports appended)
- `[FIX_BASE_SHA]` — the head the previous review saw
- `[HEAD_SHA]` — current commit
- `[DIFF_FILE]` — the path `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` printed

**Re-reviewer returns:** per-finding verdicts (ADDRESSED / NOT ADDRESSED),
new breakage in the fix diff, out-of-scope observations, and a round verdict.

Since `Value::as_object()` returns `None` for every non-object JSON type (`String`, `Number`, `Bool`, `Null`, `Array`), the fall-through is closed for all of them, not just the string case named in the finding.

## Check 1: Fall-through genuinely closed on every path
Confirmed by direct read of the current file (`extras.rs:40-72`, matches the diff exactly). The `None` arm (lines 56-67) only logs `tracing::warn!` and does nothing else; the `Some(obj)` arm (lines 43-55) is behaviorally unchanged from pre-fix (still ends by `body.insert("metadata", Value::Object(merged))`). No other branch in `apply()` touches the `"metadata"` key.

## Check 2: Would the new test fail against pre-fix code?
Traced `extra_body_non_object_metadata_is_ignored_and_builder_metadata_and_tags_survive` (`extras.rs:174-204`) against the pre-fix logic: `Extras{ metadata: {trace_id:"t-1"}, tags:["team:research"], extra_body:{"metadata":"x"} }`. Pre-fix, `body["metadata"]` is first set to `{trace_id:"t-1", tags:["team:research"]}`, then the loop's `if let Some(obj) = v.as_object()` fails (string isn't an object), falls through to `body.insert("metadata", "x".clone())`, overwriting it with the bare string `"x"`. Under that result, `v["metadata"].is_object()` is `false` and `v["metadata"]["trace_id"]` indexes a non-object `Value` (returns `Value::Null`, not `"t-1"`) — both assertions in the test would fail. The test genuinely proves the fix. The test sets both a builder `.metadata()` entry (`trace_id`) and `.tags()` (`team:research`) and asserts both survive, matching the finding's requirement.

The companion coverage gap (well-formed-object case for `metadata.tags`) is filled by the renamed `extra_body_metadata_deep_merges_with_builder_metadata_and_tags` (`extras.rs:150-172`), which adds a `tags` assertion to the pre-existing deep-merge test — this passes under both pre- and post-fix code (as expected, since that path wasn't buggy), so it's purely closing the coverage gap, not the regression itself.

## Tests / snapshot claim
Report names `cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-providers-litellm extras::tests` → 9 passed, and the file contains exactly 9 `#[test]` functions in `mod tests` — count matches. Diff stat (`review-ab5b0820..92b5e5e6.diff` line 7-8): `1 file changed, 65 insertions(+), 13 deletions(-)`, only `extras.rs` — no `.snap` file appears in the diff, corroborating the "no snapshot exercises `extra_body.metadata`" claim independent of the report's prose.

### New Breakage in the Fix Diff
None. The diff is scoped to `extras.rs`'s `metadata` branch and its test module; no other files touched, no new `pub`/reachable surface added that would perturb the parked dead_code count, no new warnings introduced (`tracing` already in use elsewhere in this crate, e.g. `translate/mod.rs`'s `tracing::warn!`).

### Out-of-Scope Observations
None.

### Verdict
**Fix round:** All findings addressed, no new Critical/Important breakage.
Task 6 closed — the fix covers all non-object JSON types, not just the string case named.

You are implementing Task 7 of a 13-task plan adding the `paigasus-helikon-providers-litellm` crate to a Rust workspace. Task 7 adds the SSE chunk types and the streaming translator. **This is the highest-risk task in the plan** — two invariants below were established by capturing real traffic from a live LiteLLM 1.97.0 proxy, and getting either wrong produces a bug that passes naive tests.

WORKING DIRECTORY (a git worktree — work only here, never in the parent checkout):
/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-451-providers-litellm

You are already on the correct branch.

## Read this first — it is your requirements
/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-451-providers-litellm/.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-16-sma-451-litellm-provider/task-7-brief.md

It contains the complete code for `src/sse.rs` and `src/stream.rs`, including 17 tests. This is a TDD task: write the tests first, watch them fail, then implement.

## Interfaces this task produces (Task 9 depends on these exact names)
- `sse::StreamChunk` (+ `Choice`, `Delta`, `ToolCallChunk`, `FunctionChunk`, `Usage`, `PromptTokensDetails`, `CompletionTokensDetails`), all `pub(crate)`
- `stream::ChatTranslator::new()`, `::consume(&mut self, chunk: StreamChunk) -> Vec<ModelEvent>`, `::finish(&mut self) -> Vec<ModelEvent>`

## The two invariants that carry this task

**1. `Finish` is emitted ONLY from `finish()`, never inline from `consume()`.**

This is not a style preference. Captured from a live proxy, the tail of a real stream is:

```
data: {…"choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{},"finish_reason":"stop"}]}
data: {…"choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{}}],"usage":{"completion_tokens":6,"prompt_tokens":8,…}}
data: [DONE]
```

The usage snapshot arrives in a **separate chunk AFTER** the one carrying `finish_reason`. `paigasus_helikon_core`'s contract states "`Finish` is the terminal event; nothing follows it". So any design that emits `Finish` inline emits `Finish` then `Usage` on **every single turn** — a contract violation, not an edge case. `consume()` must buffer the finish reason; only `finish()` may emit `Finish`.

`finish()` must emit **nothing** when no `finish_reason` was ever observed. Fabricating `Finish::Stop` on a truncated stream would make a dropped connection indistinguishable from a clean completion — and because `ModelTurnAccumulator` defaults to `Stop`, the truncated text would be committed to session history as final.

**2. Tool-call `name`/`arguments` are buffered until the `id` is known.**

The id is NOT guaranteed to arrive on the first delta, and both `name` and `arguments` fragment across deltas (`"sea"` + `"rch"` → `"search"`). The translator needs the three-map state machine in the brief. `name` must be emitted exactly once per call.

The correlation key falls back in this order: `index` when present → `id` when present → position within `delta.tool_calls`. The positional branch logs at `debug` when taken.

## Other required behaviours
- Chunk types must be genuinely permissive: `#[serde(default)]` on EVERY field including `choices`. Measured shapes the types must absorb: the first delta carries an extra `role`; the finish chunk has `delta: {}`; the trailing usage chunk has `choices:[{"index":0,"delta":{}}]` with NO `finish_reason` key; `usage` had `completion_tokens_details` but NO `prompt_tokens_details` at all — so the whole sub-object may be absent, not merely its field.
- `delta.reasoning_content` maps to `ReasoningDelta`, with `delta.reasoning` as a fallback spelling.
- Finish-reason mapping is lenient: `stop`/`length`/`tool_calls`/`function_call`/`content_filter` map to their variants; **anything else maps to `FinishReason::Other(s)`**. This leniency is the whole reason this crate does not use `async-openai`'s closed enum.
- Only the FIRST choice is read (`n > 1` returns multiple choices on this proxy — verified). Warn once when more than one is present.
- Empty `content` emits nothing.

## Global constraints
- `missing_docs` is `warn` workspace-wide and the docs CI job runs `-D warnings`. Doc-comment every item you add.
- Commit format `<type>(providers): SMA-451 <lowercase subject>`, scope MUST be `providers`.
- NEVER `git add -A` / `git add .` — `.env` and `.claude` are untracked but NOT gitignored. Stage explicit paths.
- Run `cargo fmt --all` before committing.

## Known cross-task state — do not try to fix, do not suppress
`cargo clippy -p paigasus-helikon-providers-litellm --all-targets -- -D warnings` currently fails with 14 `dead_code` errors (the plan's temporary `LiteLlmModel` shim plus the whole translation chain). Task 9 is the consumer that makes them live. Your new types will likely add more for the same structural reason. Do NOT add `#[allow(dead_code)]`. Report the count you observe.

## How to work
- Work SYNCHRONOUSLY and in the FOREGROUND. Do not background any cargo command, do not hand a long build to a monitor, and do not end your turn until the task is committed or you are genuinely blocked. Cargo commands here take minutes — wait for them.
- Do NOT run any git command that moves HEAD or branches (`checkout`, `switch`, `reset`, `rebase`, `stash`). Other sessions share this repository. `git add <paths>`, `git commit`, `git status`, `git diff`, `git log` are fine.
- If the brief's code does not compile as written, report exactly what failed. A small mechanical fix (missing import, type annotation, a `#[non_exhaustive]` catch-all arm) is fine — say so in your report. Note `ModelEvent` and `FinishReason` in core are `#[non_exhaustive]`, which may matter when matching.

/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-451-providers-litellm/.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-16-sma-451-litellm-provider/task-7-report.md

It does **not** cheat by co-locating usage on the finish chunk. Against an inline-`Finish` implementation the event vector would be `[TokenDelta, Finish, Usage]`, and the `matches!(last, ModelEvent::Finish{..})` assertion at :306 fails. The test genuinely discriminates. ✅

Name survives, concatenates, emitted once. ✅

- The hard invariant is implemented at the right level: `finish_reason` is stored as the raw `String` and mapped only in `finish()` (`stream.rs:109` vs `:204`), so there is no intermediate `FinishReason` value lying around that a future edit could accidentally emit inline. Single construction site.

### Issues

#### Critical (Must Fix)

None.

#### Important (Should Fix)

**1. `Key::Position` can never resolve a `call_id`; the spec's positional fallback is structurally inert and silently drops tool-call fragments.**
`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-litellm/src/stream.rs:132-142` + `:148-152` + `:154-164`

The only write into `self.tool_calls` is at :148, guarded by `if let Some(id) = tc.id.as_deref()`. But `Key::Position(pos)` is constructed only in the `(None, None)` arm at :135 — i.e. *only when `tc.id` is `None`*. When `tc.id` is `Some` and `tc.index` is `None`, the key is `Key::Id(...)` (:134), not `Key::Position(...)`. Therefore `tool_calls` can never contain a `Key::Position` entry, `self.tool_calls.get(&key)` at :154 is unconditionally `None` for a positional key, and every such delta takes the buffer-and-return branch at :156-163. The emit at :187 is unreachable for `Key::Position`.

Failure scenario: any tool-call delta arriving with neither `index` nor `id` — either a whole stream from a backend that omits both, or a continuation delta after an indexed/id'd first delta — accumulates its `name`/`arguments` into `self.pending` and is never emitted. The turn reaches the agent loop with a tool call whose arguments are truncated or with no tool call at all. The brief explicitly required "`index` → `id` → position within `delta.tool_calls`" as a working fallback chain; the third link is dead. Note the defect originates in the brief's own code (copied verbatim), so the design fix is the controller's call, not a coding slip.

**(b) The loss is silent.** `finish()` (`stream.rs:200-212`) never inspects `self.pending`, so a call that was buffered and never resolved vanishes with no diagnostic above `debug`. This is what would make the above indistinguishable from "the model didn't call a tool."

Fix: make the last-resort branch correlate against the key space that can actually resolve — e.g. `(None, None) => Key::Index(pos as u32)`, which matches OpenAI-compat semantics (array position *is* the index) and lets a positional continuation delta join a call already keyed by `Index`. That removes the `Position` variant entirely. Independently, add a `tracing::warn!` in `finish()` when `!self.pending.is_empty()`, naming the unresolved keys, so any future variant of this failure is visible.

#### Minor (Nice to Have)

**2. An empty-string `reasoning_content` suppresses the `reasoning` fallback.**
`stream.rs:91-95`. `.as_deref().or(delta.reasoning.as_deref()).filter(|s| !s.is_empty())` filters *after* the `or`, so `{"reasoning_content": "", "reasoning": "alt"}` yields `Some("")` → filtered → nothing emitted, and the fallback spelling never gets a chance. A backend that pads `reasoning_content` with empty strings on every delta while carrying content in `reasoning` would lose all reasoning output. Fix: `delta.reasoning_content.as_deref().filter(|s| !s.is_empty()).or_else(|| delta.reasoning.as_deref().filter(|s| !s.is_empty()))`.

**3. `finish()` does not reset the tool-call state, so a reused translator misattributes silently.**
`stream.rs:200-212` clears only `finish_reason`; `tool_calls`, `name_emitted` and `pending` survive. The doc at `stream.rs:44-46` says one instance per response, so this is not a leak today — but if Task 9 reuses an instance across turns, response 2's `Key::Index(0)` inherits response 1's `call_id` (:154 returns the stale id) *and* its `name_emitted` entry (:176 suppresses the new name), producing tool calls attributed to a previous turn's id with no name. Silent and catastrophic. Cheap insurance: clear all four fields in `finish()`, or have Task 9 take the translator by value.

**4. No test covers the neither-`index`-nor-`id` shape** — the exact gap that let finding 1 through. `tool_call_without_index_falls_back_to_id` (`stream.rs:494-506`) covers `Key::Id`; nothing covers `Key::Position`. A test feeding `{"function": {"name":"f","arguments":"{}"}}` with no `index`/`id` and asserting a `ToolCallDelta` is emitted would fail today.

**5. The warn-once flag is untested.** `warned_multi_choice` (`stream.rs:75-82`) is only observable through `tracing`; `only_the_first_choice_is_read` (`stream.rs:509`) exercises the `>1` path but asserts nothing about the warning. The flag could be permanently `true` (warning never fires) and every test still passes. A `tracing-test` subscriber assertion would close it, if the workspace already carries one.

**6. `#[serde(default)]` covers missing keys but not explicit JSON `null`.** `sse.rs:17` (`choices: Vec<Choice>`) and `sse.rs:79/81` (`prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens`: `u32`) will fail the whole chunk on `{"choices": null}` or `{"prompt_tokens": null}`. Not in any measured shape, and the module doc's permissiveness rationale (`sse.rs:3-7`) arguably promises more than this. If it matters, `Option<u32>` with `.unwrap_or(0)` at the mapping site, or `deserialize_with = "serde_with::DefaultOnNull"`.

**7. No test parses a realistic full frame.** Every fixture is a minimal synthetic object; none carries the `id`/`object`/`created`/`model`/`system_fingerprint` keys a real LiteLLM chunk sends. Serde's ignore-unknown default guarantees this works, and `stream.rs:242` does exercise one unknown key (`role`), so this is coverage polish rather than risk.

### Assessment

**Task quality:** Needs fixes

**Reasoning:** Both headline invariants are correctly implemented and — crucially — the ordering test is built on the real captured fixture shape, so it genuinely discriminates against an inline-`Finish` implementation; the clippy deviation is verifiably behaviour-preserving. The blocker is that the third link of the spec-mandated tool-call correlation chain (`Key::Position`) can provably never emit, so any delta lacking both `index` and `id` has its name and arguments silently discarded with no diagnostic.

The reviewer found a genuine defect **in my plan**, not in the implementation: `Key::Position` is provably unreachable. It's only constructed when `tc.id` is `None`, but `tool_calls` is only ever written when `tc.id` is `Some` — so a positional key never resolves, and those deltas buffer forever and are silently dropped.

That's a design decision the plan got wrong, so it's yours to settle rather than mine to patch.

Task 7 review came back "Needs fixes" with one Important finding. Both headline invariants were verified correct — this is a defect in the brief's own code, not in your work, and the project owner has already decided the fix. Apply it, re-run the covering tests, and append a fix report to your existing report file.

---

**Important — `Key::Position` can never resolve a `call_id`; the spec's positional fallback is structurally inert and silently drops tool-call fragments.** `src/stream.rs:132-142`, `:148-152`, `:154-164`.

The only write into `self.tool_calls` is at `:148`, guarded by `if let Some(id) = tc.id.as_deref()`. But `Key::Position(pos)` is constructed only in the `(None, None)` arm at `:135` — i.e. *only when `tc.id` is `None`*. When `tc.id` is `Some` and `tc.index` is `None`, the key is `Key::Id(...)`, not `Key::Position(...)`. So `tool_calls` can never contain a `Key::Position` entry, `self.tool_calls.get(&key)` at `:154` is unconditionally `None` for a positional key, every such delta takes the buffer-and-return branch at `:156-163`, and the emit at `:187` is unreachable for `Key::Position`.

Failure scenario: any tool-call delta arriving with neither `index` nor `id` — a continuation delta after an indexed first delta, or a whole stream from a backend that omits both — accumulates its `name`/`arguments` into `self.pending` and is never emitted. The turn reaches the agent loop with a truncated tool call, or none at all. And the loss is silent: `finish()` never inspects `self.pending`, so it is indistinguishable from "the model didn't call a tool."

---

**The decided fix** (chosen by the project owner from three options):

1. **Delete the `Key::Position` variant entirely.** Change the `(None, None)` arm to `Key::Index(pos as u32)`. In OpenAI-compatible streaming the array position *is* the index, so a positional continuation delta correctly joins a call already keyed by `Index`. Keep the `tracing::debug!` on that branch, since it is still a fallback worth seeing.

2. **Add a `tracing::warn!` in `finish()` when `self.pending` is not empty**, naming the unresolved keys. This is deliberate and load-bearing: fix (1) does not help a backend that never sends `id` at all — that stream still buffers with nothing emitted — and the point of the warning is to make that residual case loud instead of silent. Emit it before the `Finish` event (or before the early return when no finish reason was buffered — it should fire on both paths).

3. **Add the test the reviewer identified as missing**, which is the gap that let this through: feed a delta carrying `{"function": {"name": "f", "arguments": "{}"}}` with neither `index` nor `id`, plus a second delta that supplies the `id`, and assert a `ToolCallDelta` is actually emitted with the buffered name and args intact. Confirm this test FAILS against the current code before your fix and passes after — say so explicitly in your report.

Note the spec's prose ("use `index` when present; else `id` when present; else the position of the entry") remains accurate under this fix — only the brief's implementation sketch was wrong. No spec change is needed.

Do NOT change anything else. In particular do not attempt to fix the parked clippy `dead_code` errors (Task 9 is their consumer), and do not add `#[allow(dead_code)]`.

Work synchronously and in the foreground; do not background cargo. Do not run any git command that moves HEAD or branches. Name the covering tests you ran, the exact command, and its output in your fix report. Then reply with: STATUS, commit SHA(s), one line of test results, and any concerns.

The Task 7 review is worth reading as a vindication of the process. Both headline invariants came back verified — `Finish` is constructed at exactly one site inside `finish()`, and the ordering test uses the *real captured fixture shape* (separate trailing usage chunk), so it genuinely discriminates against an inline-`Finish` implementation. The three-way tool-call correlation chain I specified — `index` → `id` → position — has an unreachable third link, because I keyed positional fallback on `tc.id` being absent while making resolution depend on `tc.id` being present. Deltas with neither field buffer forever and vanish silently. You chose position-becomes-index plus a `finish()` warning, so the residual "backend never sends `id`" case is at least loud.

- **It originated in the spec/plan, not the implementation.** Two reviewers and a live-proxy verification pass didn't catch it; it took an adversarial read of the state machine against a concrete failure trace. The plan's own §9.3 prose was right — the code sketch under it wasn't.
- **The missing test is what let it through.** There was coverage for `Key::Id` and `Key::Index`, none for the neither-field case. The fix dispatch requires that test to be demonstrated red-before-green.

Also parked for Task 9: the translator doesn't reset `tool_calls`/`name_emitted`/`pending` in `finish()`. Harmless as long as Task 9 constructs a fresh `ChatTranslator` inside `invoke()` — which the plan does specify — but if it ever reused one, turn 2's tool calls would silently inherit turn 1's `call_id` and suppress its own name. That's now an explicit constraint on Task 9's dispatch rather than a latent trap.

Fix round 2. The scoped re-review confirmed all three prescribed parts of round 1 landed correctly, and traced your new regression test as genuinely red pre-fix. But it found that the fix itself introduced new Important breakage. This one is on the fix design, not on you executing it.

```json
{"choices": [{"index": 0, "delta": {"tool_calls": [
    {"index": 1, "id": "y", "function": {"name": "g", "arguments": "{}"}},
    {"function": {"name": "f", "arguments": "{}"}}
]}}]}
```

Entry 0 (`pos=0`) has explicit `index: 1` → `Key::Index(1)`; it resolves immediately via `id: "y"`, emits, and marks `Key::Index(1)` in `name_emitted`. Entry 1 (`pos=1`) has neither `index` nor `id` → the `(None, None)` arm produces `Key::Index(pos as u32)` = `Key::Index(1)` — **the same key**, because the loop already mutated `tool_calls` and `name_emitted` for it earlier in the same iteration. It never enters `pending`, so `warn_unresolved_pending` cannot see it.

Before round 1, `Key::Position(1)` and `Key::Index(1)` were distinct variants and could not collide — the old bug was 100% loss, not corruption. Round 1 traded total loss for silent corruption, which is worse. No existing test constructs a mixed-entry chunk.

---

**The fix for round 2** — keep the human's decision intact for the case it was chosen for, and close the collision:

**Apply the positional fallback only when NO entry in the same `delta.tool_calls` array carries an explicit `index`.**

Concretely: before the per-entry loop, scan the array once — e.g. `let any_explicit_index = tcs.iter().any(|tc| tc.index.is_some());`. Pass that into the key resolution. Then:

- `(Some(i), _)` → `Key::Index(i)` (unchanged)
- `(None, Some(id))` → `Key::Id(id)` (unchanged)
- `(None, None)` and `!any_explicit_index` → `Key::Index(pos as u32)`, keeping the existing `tracing::debug!`
- `(None, None)` and `any_explicit_index` → **ambiguous**: emit a `tracing::warn!` naming the position, and skip the entry entirely (do not buffer it into `pending`, do not emit).

Verdict on the finding under verification, followed by diff inspection.

### Finding Verdicts

- **Collapsing the positional fallback into `Key::Index`'s number space lets a synthesized key collide with a genuine explicit `index`, silently merging two distinct tool calls.** — ADDRESSED. `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-litellm/src/stream.rs:116` computes `any_explicit_index = tcs.iter().any(|tc| tc.index.is_some())` once, before the per-entry loop, over the whole `tcs` array — so the flag is order-independent (an explicit index appearing after the ambiguous entry in array order is still seen, since the scan covers the full array up front). `stream.rs:156-171` adds a guarded match arm `(None, None) if any_explicit_index` that logs a `tracing::warn!` and `return`s before any state mutation. The original `(None, None)` fallback (`stream.rs:172-179`, `Key::Index(pos as u32)`) now only fires when `!any_explicit_index`, i.e. when the whole array is unindexed — exactly the "genuine continuation" case.

### Hard-check results

1. **Collision closed for every mixed-array shape** — Yes. Traced three variants by hand against the code: (a) explicit index *after* the index-less entry — closed, because `any_explicit_index` is computed by scanning the full array before the loop starts, not incrementally, so processing order is irrelevant; (b) two index-less entries alongside one explicit-index entry — both index-less entries independently hit the guarded arm and are skipped/warned, no collision possible since neither ever reaches `self.tool_calls`; (c) an index-less entry whose position doesn't numerically match any explicit index in the same array — still skipped (the guard fires on "any explicit index present," not "this position specifically collides"), which is conservative but matches the prescribed recipe verbatim ("apply the positional fallback only when NO entry in the same array carries an explicit index"), not a bug.
2. **Warn-and-skip leaks nothing** — Confirmed. The `return` at `stream.rs:170` sits inside the match arm that produces `key`, before `name_frag`/`args_frag` extraction (`stream.rs:182-183`), before the `self.tool_calls` insert (`stream.rs:185-189`), and before the `pending` buffer (`stream.rs:191-201`). A skipped entry touches no state at all.
3. **Collision test genuinely fails against round-1 code** — Confirmed by manual trace. Input `[{"index":1,"id":"y",...name:"g"...}, {no index/no id, name:"f"}]` against round-1 logic (`(None, None) => Key::Index(pos as u32)` unconditionally): entry 0 inserts `tool_calls[Key::Index(1)] = "y"` and `name_emitted.insert(Key::Index(1))`, emitting one `ToolCallDelta{call_id:"y", name:Some("g"), args_delta:"{}"}`. Entry 1 (`pos=1`) synthesizes the same `Key::Index(1)`, finds it already resolved to `"y"` in `tool_calls`, so it does *not* buffer — it flows through the resolve path, `name_emitted` already contains the key so its own name `"f"` is swallowed, and it emits a second `ToolCallDelta{call_id:"y", name:None, args_delta:"{}"}`. Two events, both `call_id:"y"` — matches the report's claimed `left: 2, right: 1` exactly, and confirms genuine corruption (not just a count mismatch).
4. **Continuation regression guard is a real guard** — Confirmed. In `unindexed_continuation_after_an_indexed_first_delta_still_joins` (`stream.rs:648`), the second `consume()` call's `tool_calls` array has exactly one entry with neither `index` nor `id`, so `any_explicit_index` is `false` for that call and the entry falls through to the unconditional `Key::Index(pos as u32) = Key::Index(0)` arm, joining the call opened by the first chunk's explicit `index:0`. Traced against round-1 code too (no guard existed there, so the same unconditional arm applied) — it also passes, confirming true "before and after" behavior. If the fallback were later made unconditional-skip, this second fragment would never emit and the joined-args assertion (`"{\"x\": 1}"`) would fail — the guard has teeth.

### New Breakage in the Fix Diff

None.

### Out-of-Scope Observations

Minor, non-blocking: no dedicated test exercises the case where an index-less entry appears *before* an explicit-index entry in the same array (check 1a's reverse ordering) or the two-ambiguous-entries case (check 1b) — both are handled correctly by the precomputed, order-independent `any_explicit_index` flag per the code trace above, so this is a test-coverage gap rather than a functional gap.

### Verdict

**Fix round:** All findings addressed, no new Critical/Important breakage.

This is the wiring task: it replaces a temporary shim with the real `LiteLlmModel`, implements `paigasus_helikon_core::Model`, and connects a request builder, a JSON translator, an SSE framer, a streaming translator and an error classifier into one HTTP path. It is where the parts meet, so integration mistakes surface here or not at all.

## What Was Requested

Read the task brief: /Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-451-providers-litellm/.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-16-sma-451-litellm-provider/task-9-brief.md

Global constraints that bind this task:

- **Check HTTP status and `content-type` BEFORE entering SSE framing.** Measured against a live LiteLLM 1.97.0 proxy: a failing streaming request returns `HTTP 500` with `content-type: application/json` and a plain JSON error body — NOT an SSE stream carrying an error frame. Only a 2xx `text/event-stream` response may enter the framing loop.
- **A FRESH `ChatTranslator` must be constructed inside `invoke()`, per call.** `ChatTranslator::finish()` does not reset `tool_calls`/`name_emitted`/`pending`, so a translator reused across turns would resolve turn 2's tool calls to turn 1's `call_id` and suppress their names — silently. It must not become a field on the model.
- **`translator.finish()` must be called at BOTH `[DONE]` and stream EOF.** Missing either loses the terminal `Finish` event.
- **Cancellation**: `tokio::select!` with `biased` on the cancel arm, at both the request future and each upstream poll. Per core's contract a cancelled stream ends WITHOUT emitting `Finish`.
- **Correlation logging**: `x-litellm-call-id` / `x-litellm-model-id` plus the `attempted-retries` / `attempted-fallbacks` headers at `tracing::debug!`, with the call id attached to error context. These headers were verified present on streaming responses too.
- `provider()` returns `"litellm"`; `model()` returns the alias verbatim.
- The mid-stream `data: {"error": …}` handling is **defensive and unverified** — every reproducible failure returns non-2xx JSON before the stream opens.
- `missing_docs` is `warn` workspace-wide and docs CI runs `-D warnings`: every `pub` item needs a `///` doc comment.
- Commit format `<type>(providers): SMA-451 <lowercase subject>`, scope MUST be `providers`.

**The hard gate on this task**: before it, `cargo clippy -p paigasus-helikon-providers-litellm --all-targets -- -D warnings` failed with 31 `dead_code` errors, because nothing outside `#[cfg(test)]` called the translation/streaming/error chain. `Model::invoke` is the consumer that makes them live. The implementer was told that any surviving `dead_code` is a real finding, not a transient, and that suppressing it with `#[allow(dead_code)]` or by deleting items was forbidden.
